newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-MONTGOMERIE READY FOR MASTERS BREAKTHROUGH.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-MONTGOMERIE READY FOR MASTERS BREAKTHROUGH.

text.p: Colin Montgomerie, the best golfer on the European tour for the past four years, has finally realised what it takes to win the Masters, the one major championship in which he has failed to perform well.
"You never find a bad putter winning here," Montgomerie said Wednesday morning before heading off for his final practice before the Masters begins Thursday.

"You can't win here not holing putts," the big Briton added for emphasis as he discussed why he thought this year may mark his breakthrough at Augusta National, where his best Masters finish was joint 17th two years ago.

The 33-year-old Scot was so intent on improving his record in the Masters that he sought out Ryder Cup rival Brad Faxon to play a practice round so he could observe the American's putting technique and pick his brain about Augusta's huge, rolling greens, which may be the fastest in the world.
"It's amazing how much break you have to give these putts," Montgomerie said.

"On ultra-fast greens 85 percent of missed putts are on the low side," he added. "That means either your pace was wrong or you mis-read the line. You're not going to make any putts hitting them on the low side."

Montgomerie, who has top-10 finishes in the other three major championships -- incuding playoff losses in the U.S. Open and PGA Championship -- said his putting was one of several factors that gave him added confidence going into the year's first major.
"I'm putting quite well," he said. "I've putted better in practice here than ever before."
Montgomerie, who played four consecutive tournaments in the United States to prepare for the Masters, finishing in the top 20 in each, also said there were other reasons for his confidence this week.

"Coming in here I've never hit the ball better," he said. "I'm looking forward to competing in this tournament for the first time. This is the first year that I will actually compete," he added, putting emphasis on the last word.
Montgomerie, whose professional record has been one of almost constant improvement, has shot only two rounds in the 60s at Augusta -- a pair of 69s in his best showing in 1995.
"I haven't coped so well here so far," he admitted. "I've been frustrated with Augusta over the years."
Montgomerie did not even break par 72 last year, when he tied for 39th.

"I am a better player than I was last year," he insisted. "I am hitting the ball right to left with ease" -- a shot that is required to play Augusta well, as Jack Nicklaus proved over the years in winning six green jackets.
Montgomerie, who said Faxon's positive approach to the game rubbed off on him during their practice round, even found a good omen in his starting time for Thursday.
"I've got a good time tomorrow," he said. "It is the first time that I've started here before 1:30 (p.m.)." He was scheduled to tee off with Davis Love at 11:56 a.m. (1556 GMT).
Players who start late often encounter more difficult conditions than earlier starters -- including more spike marks on the greens and more challenging weather conditions.
"Tomorrow will be vital for me to put a 69 or 70 on the board," Montgomerie said. "Tomorrow is a very important day."
